## Context

Primer React components was originally released without TypeScript type definitions, making it difficult for engineers to consume the library in TypeScript applications. In [July 2019](https://github.com/primer/react/commit/2983c935ea9ad600c04078adb25e40c3624c11fa#diff-7aa4473ede4abd9ec099e87fec67fd57afafaf39e05d493ab4533acc38547eb8), we created an [ambient declaration](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/typescript-ambients-declaration/) file (`index.d.ts`) file to provide type definitions for TypeScript applications without having to rewrite Primer React components in TypeScript.

`index.d.ts` has been an effective stopgap, enabling teams to build complex applications with Primer React components and TypeScript. However, because `index.d.ts` is disconnected from the implementation code, we've struggled to keep the type definitions up-to-date and accurate, as evidenced by [many](https://github.com/primer/react/issues/906) [TypeScript](https://github.com/primer/react/issues/540) [bug](https://github.com/primer/react/issues/520) [reports](https://github.com/primer/react/issues/534). As the library continues to grow in size and complexity, manually maintaining type definitions will become unsustainable.
decision:
## Decision
We will migrate the Primer React component library from JavaScript to TypeScript.

This migration will ensure that our type definitions are always accurate and up-to-date, as they will be inferred directly from the component implementations. This solves the primary problem of maintaining a separate, manually-created `index.d.ts` file and eliminates the class of bugs related to out-of-sync types.

The migration will be gradual:
1.  All **new** components will be written in TypeScript (`.tsx`).
2.  Existing JavaScript components will be converted to TypeScript incrementally. We will prioritize migrating the most commonly used and complex components first to provide the greatest immediate benefit to consumers.
3.  We will configure our build process to compile TypeScript and generate declaration files automatically, ensuring that consumers always receive the most accurate types.
4.  Once the entire library is converted, the manually-maintained `index.d.ts` file will be removed.

## Context

`Drafts` were introduced in [ADR-006](./adrs/adr-006-drafts.md) as a way of creating components outside of the root bundle of `@primer/react`. This helps us create, test and maintain multiple versions of the same component in parallel.

Example:

```js
// default version of component exported from root of package
import {UnderlineNav} from '@primer/react'

// new version of component exported from /drafts
import {UnderlineNav} from '@primer/react/drafts'
```

We have also used this method for components that are still a work in progress and we don't want developers to start using them in production without collaborating with us first.

Example:

```js
// this component only exists in drafts and not in the roof of the package
import {TreeView} from '@primer/react/drafts'
```
decision:
## Decision
We will formalize the use of a `/drafts` export path (`@primer/react/drafts`) for components that are not yet considered part of the stable, public API of the library. This provides a clear mechanism for shipping experimental work without committing to semantic versioning guarantees for those specific components.

Components in `/drafts` fall into two categories:

1.  **Next-generation versions of existing components:** When creating a new, potentially breaking version of a stable component (like `UnderlineNav`), the new version will be developed and exported from `/drafts`. This allows consumers to opt-in and test the new version while the stable version remains the default export from the package root. Once the new version is deemed stable, it can be promoted to the root in a future major release.

2.  **New, unstable components:** Brand new components that are still under heavy development or have an unstable API (like `TreeView`) will be exported exclusively from `/drafts`. This signals to consumers that the component is a work-in-progress, its API is subject to change without notice, and it should not be used in production without explicit collaboration with the core team.

**Implications for Consumers:**
*   Any component imported from `@primer/react/drafts` is considered unstable.
*   The APIs of these components are not bound by SemVer and may introduce breaking changes in any release.
*   Consumers should use these components at their own risk and expect to perform migrations if they are used in long-lived applications.
*   Once a component "graduates" from `/drafts` to the main package export, it will be considered stable and will follow our standard versioning and deprecation policies.

context: ## Context [Snapshot testing](https://jestjs.io/docs/snapshot-testing) is a strategy that allows a developer to "snapshot" a given value within a test suite. This value could be a primitive within JavaScript, an Array, an object, or the resulting HTML of rendering a component in React. The snapshot of the value is stored within the repo and is then compared against future test runs. When a change is detected to a snapshot, the test will fail with a diff between the currently stored snapshot and the new snapshot. Within the space of React components, this may happen when a class name changes or the markup of a component changes. Is is then up to the developer to decide if the change is intentional and whether or not to accept this new snapshot as the baseline for future test runs. A common practice is to snapshot a React component which will capture the HTML output of rendering a component. For example: ```jsx import renderer from 'react-test-renderer' import Link from '../Link' it('renders correctly', () => { const tree = renderer.create(Facebook).toJSON() expect(tree).toMatchSnapshot() }) ``` ```js exports[`renders correctly 1`] = ` Facebook ` ``` [Source](https://jestjs.io/docs/snapshot-testing#snapshot-testing-with-jest) As the number of snapshots within a project grows, there are a couple of challenges that emerge: - Components with wide or deep trees emit large snapshots - Debugging what change lead to a broken snapshot can be difficult - It is unclear what the intent may be of a snapshot test when something does fail, in other words it does not always answer the question: what is this testing?
decision:
## Decision
We will avoid using snapshot testing for React components.

While snapshot tests can be useful for quickly capturing the output of a component, they suffer from several drawbacks that make them unsuitable for our project's goals of clarity and maintainability:

1.  **Brittleness:** Snapshots are sensitive to any change in the component's markup, including non-functional changes like adding a wrapper `div` for styling or changing a class name. This leads to frequent, low-value test failures.
2.  **Lack of Intent:** A snapshot test with the description "it renders correctly" does not communicate *what* aspect of the component is important. When it fails, it is difficult to determine if the change was intentional or an accidental regression without a manual, time-consuming review of a potentially large diff.
3.  **Poor Debugging Experience:** Large component trees result in large snapshot files. A small change can cause a large diff, making it difficult to pinpoint the root cause of the failure.

Instead of snapshot tests, we will favor writing tests with explicit assertions that focus on the behavior and essential output of a component, primarily using libraries like React Testing Library. This approach tests components from the user's perspective.

For example, instead of:

```jsx
it('renders correctly', () => {
  const tree = renderer.create(<Link page="http://www.facebook.com">Facebook</Link>).toJSON()
  expect(tree).toMatchSnapshot()
})
```

We will write:

```jsx
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react'
import Link from '../Link'

it('renders a link with the correct text and href', () => {
  render(<Link page="http://www.facebook.com">Facebook</Link>)
  
  const linkElement = screen.getByRole('link', { name: /facebook/i })
  
  expect(linkElement).toBeInTheDocument()
  expect(linkElement).toHaveAttribute('href', 'http://www.facebook.com')
})
```

This approach makes our tests more resilient, readable, and maintainable. The intent of the test is clear, and when it fails, it will point directly to the specific behavior that has broken.

## Context

There are situations where we would like to provide warnings to developers who
use `@primer/react` that something may be deprecated, unsupported, etc. Often,
these will be emitted using `console.warn()`. When using `console.warn()` by
itself, we run into a situation where code that is only meant for development
is included in production code. As a result, it would be helpful to establish
patterns around how to provide warnings to developers in order to make sure
that:

- Calls to `console.warn()` do not appear in production
- Code related to development checks, warnings, or messages are removed from
  production code
predicted_decision:
## Decision

Code that is meant for development-only warnings or checks **must** be wrapped within a
`__DEV__` block.

```tsx
function ExampleComponent() {
  if (__DEV__) {
    // This code only runs in development
  }
}
```

Under-the-hood, the `__DEV__` block will be compiled to a `NODE_ENV` check so
that it is stripped when `NODE_ENV` is set to `'production'`.

> **Note**
> Contributors may wrap hooks within a `__DEV__` block even though hooks are not
> meant to be called conditionally. This is because the `__DEV__` check can be
> considered constant in that it will always be true or false for the
> environment (development or production).

When a contributor would like to communicate a warning to a developer, they
should use the `warning()` helper.

```ts
warning(condition, 'This is the message that is logged when condition is truth-y')
```

This helper allows you to provide a `condition`. When the condition is truth-y
it will emit the message provided. This helper is automatically wrapped in a
`__DEV__` block and will be removed from production builds.

For more complex conditions, a contributor may combine `console.warn()` with
`__DEV__` when `warning()` does not suffice.

## Context

There are several components in Primer React that make use of live regions.
However, the library does not have a central pattern for making accessible live
region announcements. This ADR documents the decision to use a central pattern
for live region announcements that can be used across Primer and GitHub.

ARIA Live regions fall into several buckets that we may want to use as component
authors:

- [ARIA live region roles](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#live_region_roles), such as `alert`, `log`, or `status`
- [The `aria-live` attribute](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#aria-live) to turn an element into a live region

In components, we see the following scenarios in Primer React:

- Announce the contents of an element when it is rendered or on page load, like when a spinner is displayed or a form is submitted
- Announce the changes to the content of an element, like when the count inside of a
  button is incremented
- Announce a message programmatically, such as the number of results for a query

Currently, contributors may reach for roles such as `alert` or `status` to
achieve these scenarios. They may also add `aria-live="assertive"` or `aria-live="polite"` with an an `aria-atomic="true"` to an element explicitly.
However, both of these approaches do not announce consistently across screen
readers. This could be due to live regions being injected dynamically into the document (this includes loading content into the document via React), dynamically changing the visibility of a live region, or some other technique causing an announcement to not be announced.

For more information about the ways in which live regions may not work as
expected, visit: [Why are my live regions not working?](https://tetralogical.com/blog/2024/05/01/why-are-my-live-regions-not-working/)
decision:
## Decision 
We will implement a centralized pattern for ARIA live regions using a `LiveRegion` provider component and a `useLiveRegion` hook. This will provide a consistent, reliable, and easy-to-use API for all components in Primer React that need to make screen reader announcements.

### How it will work:
1.  **`LiveRegion` Component:** A new `LiveRegion` component will be created. This component will render a set of visually hidden `div` elements, one for each politeness level (`polite` and `assertive`). These elements will be present in the DOM from the moment the `LiveRegion` provider is mounted, avoiding the inconsistencies that arise from dynamically injecting live regions into the page. This component should be placed high in the application tree, likely within the `ThemeProvider`, to be available to all child components.

2.  **`useLiveRegion` Hook:** A new `useLiveRegion` hook will be the public API for component authors.
    - This hook will provide access to an `announce` function.
    - The `announce(message, {politeness: 'polite' | 'assertive'})` function will programmatically update the content of the appropriate persistent `div` rendered by the `LiveRegion` component.
    - The default politeness level will be `'polite'`.

### Why this approach:
-   **Reliability:** By using static, persistent elements as the live regions, we avoid common bugs where screen readers fail to announce content that is dynamically added to the DOM or has its visibility toggled.
-   **Consistency:** All live region announcements will be routed through this single, shared mechanism, ensuring consistent behavior across the entire component library.
-   **Improved Developer Experience:** Component authors will no longer need to be experts on the nuances and pitfalls of ARIA live regions. They can simply call `announce('Your message here')` to reliably have a message read by screen readers.

### Adoption Plan:
1.  Implement the `LiveRegion` component and the `useLiveRegion` hook.
2.  Add the `LiveRegion` provider to our application/documentation layout.
3.  Systematically refactor all existing components that currently use `role="alert"`, `role="status"`, or direct `aria-live` attributes to use the new `useLiveRegion` hook.
4.  Document this new pattern as the standard way to handle screen reader announcements in Primer React.

## Context

Our testing infrastructure consists of Jest "unit" tests and automatic Chromatic visual testing. Both of these are super useful but we have been experiencing a few setbacks.
Unofficially we test more complex interactive scenarios using our storybooks setup.

1. Repeated markup in storybooks and jest tests - Since there is not automation of interaction in storybooks, we tend to test them out manually in stories and then transfer to jest. This results in us constructing similar test case scenarios in storybooks and in tests.

2. Debugging complex jest tests - There is no visual aspect to jest tests. Mostly everything is CLI based. This makes it hard to debug broken tests. Visibility into these tests is also low for people who want to enhance them.
decision:
## Decision 
We will adopt Storybook's interaction testing framework to automate and consolidate our component testing. This approach allows us to write tests directly alongside our stories, using a `play` function to simulate user interactions.

This directly addresses our stated problems:

1.  **Reduces Duplication:** By co-locating interaction logic with the story setup, we eliminate the need to recreate component markup and state in separate Jest test files. The same story serves as a visual showcase, a manual test case, and an automated integration test.

2.  **Improves Debugging:** When an interaction test fails, we can open the story in a browser. Storybook provides a visual, step-by-step debugger that allows us to walk through each interaction (user events, API calls) and inspect the state of the component at every point. This is a significant improvement over the CLI-only feedback loop of Jest.

### Workflow
- For components requiring complex user interaction, we will write stories that include a `play` function.
- This function will use utilities from `@storybook/testing-library` and `@storybook/user-event` to simulate user behavior.
- Assertions will be made using `@storybook/jest`.
- These interaction tests will be run headlessly in CI using the `@storybook/test-runner`.
- Existing Jest tests that are pure unit tests (e.g., for utility functions, hooks) will remain. Jest tests that are primarily concerned with rendering and interacting with components will be migrated to Storybook interaction tests over time.

## Context

> tl;dr
>
> We have workspaces within the project but no official way of connecting them or managing dependencies from the top-level. Similarly, scripts that grow in size or complexity have no dedicated home or ability to manage dependencies outside of the top-level workspace.

The `primer/react` repo is composed of several workspaces that use `npm` to manage dependencies. In order to install these dependencies, a contributor needs to visit each directory and run `npm install`. The project also has a convenience script for this task, invoked through `npm run setup`, that goes through this process for contributors.

These distinct workspaces may sometimes depend on each other. For example, the `docs` workspace depends on the `@primer/react` package which is defined at the top-level of the project. Similarly, examples in the `examples/*` folders may also depend on `@primer/react`. Currently these dependencies are expressed either through relative paths, file dependencies in `package.json`, or symlinks through `npm link`.

There is also a collection of scripts under the `script` directory that exist in the project that involve varying levels of complexity and depth.
decision:
## Decision
We will adopt **pnpm** as our package manager and **Turborepo** as our task runner to manage the monorepo. This combination provides a robust, modern, and efficient solution to the problems of dependency management, inter-workspace linking, and script execution.

The workflow will be as follows:

1.  **Use pnpm for Dependency Management**:
    *   A single `pnpm-workspace.yaml` file at the root will define all workspaces (`packages/*`, `docs`, `examples/*`, etc.).
    *   Developers will only need to run `pnpm install` once at the project root to install all dependencies for all workspaces. `pnpm` will automatically handle hoisting dependencies and symlinking local packages.
    *   Inter-workspace dependencies (e.g., `docs` depending on `@primer/react`) will be declared with a `workspace:*` version in their respective `package.json` files, ensuring they always resolve to the local version. This replaces fragile `file:` paths and `npm link` workflows.

2.  **Use Turborepo for Task Running**:

## Context

Reasons for change: Performance, utilise css variables

The main reason for changing our styling architecture is to remove performance issues for applications:

Relevant parts from [primer/discussions#1928](https://github.com/github/primer/discussions/1928#reasons)(Hubbers only link):

1. Initial page loads take longer

   Because styles are injected during runtime, we can not parallelize this work. The page is un-styled till the javascript bundle is
   downloaded and processed. The processing time is longer on slower devices.

   Benchmarks:

   i. Lab benchmarks: rendering a page with 1000 components
   runtime injection of css: 242ms
   static .css files: 96ms (60% faster)

   ii. Application benchmarks: render times for repo directory (>1000 files, [gh/gh#241090](https://github.com/github/github/pull/241090))
   with primer/react Box: 3800ms
   with custom css: 3076ms (20% faster)

2. Slow server side rendering

   Some applications are able to make up for slower initial render times by collecting styles on the server first. In the correct stack, collecting styles requires rendering the app twice before we can ship any html to the user.

   benchmarks: in the issues-app experiment, collecting styles on the server contributed to + 20% of rendering time (450ms on top of 1900ms)

3. Style updates are expensive

   The slowest part of the current stack is updating styles based on props or state. Big changes take linearly longer, worse on slower devices.

   Benchmarks:

   i. Lab benchmarks: updating a page with 1000 components, static runtime css vs. dynamic runtime css (thanks @mattcosta7 for these!)

   re-rendering components with fixed styles on runtime: 242ms
   re-rendering components with dynamic styles on runtime: 441ms (55% slower)

   ii. Application benchmarks: opting out of IconButton for PR diff view (>500 files, [gh/gh#243269](https://github.com/github/github/pull/243269))

   dynamic styles with sx prop: 400ms
   dynamic styles with .css files: 165ms (60% faster)

The other reasons for change are to utilise css variables for theming and improve the guardrails of consuming primer/primitives
decision:
## Decision 
We will adopt a static CSS architecture, compiling styles into static `.css` files at build time. This moves style computation from runtime to build time, directly addressing the identified performance bottlenecks in initial page load, server-side rendering, and dynamic style updates.

The new architecture will be based on the following principles:
1.  **Static First**: All component styles will be compiled into static `.css` files that can be included in the application's `<head>`. This allows the browser to download and parse styles in parallel, eliminating the flash of unstyled content and significantly speeding up initial render.
2.  **CSS Variables for Dynamics**: Dynamic styling, such as theming and component state variations, will be handled primarily through CSS Custom Properties (variables). This allows for efficient, runtime changes without needing to inject, remove, or recalculate entire CSS rules in JavaScript.
3.  **Deprecation of Runtime Injection**: Mechanisms that inject styles at runtime, specifically the `sx` prop, will be deprecated and phased out.
4.  **Utility and Component Classes**: To provide clear guardrails and a consistent developer experience, we will provide a set of pre-defined utility classes and component-specific classes generated from `primer/primitives`. This offers a more constrained and performant alternative to free-form style objects.

## Context

> **Note**
> This ADR supercedes [`ADR 009`](./adr-009-interaction-tests.md)

We author tests using a combination of Jest and Playwright. Typically, Jest is
used for unit and integration tests and Playwright is used for Visual Regression
Tests against our Storybook.

In `ADR 009`, we proposed using Storybook's [`play`
functions](https://storybook.js.org/docs/react/writing-stories/play-function) as
the recommended way to author tests that require tests based on user
interactions. In this ADR, we would like to revisit this decision.
decision:
## Decision 
We will deprecate the use of Storybook `play` functions for authoring interaction tests. Instead, we will use Playwright for all tests that require simulating user interactions.

This decision is based on the following factors:

1.  **Separation of Concerns:** Storybook's primary purpose is to serve as a component workshop for development, visualization, and documentation. While `play` functions are a convenient feature, overloading Storybook with complex testing logic moves it away from its core strength. Playwright is a dedicated, powerful end-to-end testing framework built specifically for this purpose.

2.  **Tool Consolidation:** We already use Playwright for our Visual Regression Tests. Standardizing on Playwright for interaction tests as well reduces the number of testing paradigms our team needs to learn and maintain. This creates a more unified and consistent testing strategy.

3.  **More Powerful and Realistic Testing:** Playwright runs tests in a real browser environment, offering more realistic and reliable results than the JSDOM-like environment of Storybook's test runner. It is also better suited for testing complex user flows that may involve multiple components, pages, or even network requests, which are difficult or impossible to model within a single Storybook story.

4.  **Superior Debugging:** Playwright offers a first-class debugging experience, including its Trace Viewer, which provides step-by-step execution, network logs, and time-travel capabilities. This is significantly more powerful than the debugging tools available for Storybook `play` functions.

### Path Forward
- New interaction tests should be authored directly in Playwright.
- Existing tests that use Storybook `play` functions should be migrated to Playwright as they are updated or as time permits.
- Storybook `play` functions may still be used for simple setup states within a story (e.g., opening a modal by default) but not for asserting behavior.

## Context

There are situations where a component prop can support a value or a "responsive
value" that results in the value changing depending on the viewport size. For
example:

```tsx
// Value
<Stack gap="condensed" />

// Responsive value
<Stack gap={{ narrow: 'condensed', regular: 'normal', wide: 'spacious' />
```

Typically, a responsive value will support all of our named breakpoints: narrow,
regular, and wide. Authors can use a hook called `useResponsiveValue` to support
resolving the value of a prop based on the current viewport size. The
implementation of this hook uses [`matchMedia`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/matchMedia)
which, unfortunately, has a downside: the value of a prop may shift when the
component is server-side rendered. If the prop is used for styles or layout, then this will lead to a layout shift
when the component hydrates and the viewport size is different than the fallback
size on the server.

As a result, we would like to offer a paved path for providing responsive props
in a way tha twill not lead to layout shift during server-side rendering.

## Context

There are times when a prop is deprecated in favor of a more accessible API or a more flexible prop that can support a wider range of values. In these cases, we want to provide a clear path for authors to migrate from the deprecated prop to the new API.

For

```tsx

<ActionList>
  <ActionList.Group title="Group title">
    <ActionList.Item>Item 1</ActionList.Item>
    <ActionList.Item>Item 2</ActionList.Item>
  </ActionList.Group>
</ActionList>
```

```tsx
  <ActionList.Group>

    <ActionList.Item>Item 1</ActionList.Item>
    <ActionList.Item>Item 2</ActionList.Item>

</ActionList>
```

## Context

- Proxy support is required for some enterprises and organizations to start using their own self-hosted runners
- While there is not a standard convention, many applications support setting proxies via the environment variables `http_proxy`, `https_proxy`, `no_proxy`, such as curl, wget, perl, python, docker, git, and R
  - Some of these applications use `HTTPS_PROXY` versus `https_proxy`, but most understand or primarily support the lowercase variant
decision:
## Decision 
We will add support for HTTP proxies in self-hosted runners by reading proxy configuration from standard environment variables.
This allows organizations that require all outbound traffic to go through a proxy to use our runners, and it follows a well-established convention used by many other command-line tools and libraries.
Specifically, the runner process will check for and use the following environment variables:
- `http_proxy`: The URL of the proxy to use for all HTTP requests.
- `https_proxy`: The URL of the proxy to use for all HTTPS requests.
- `no_proxy`: A comma-separated list of hostnames or domains that should bypass the proxy and be connected to directly.
To maximize compatibility, we will support both the lowercase (e.g., `http_proxy`) and uppercase (e.g., `HTTP_PROXY`) versions of these variables. If both are present, the lowercase variable will take precedence.

## Decision

We will update the Runner to use the conventional environment variables for proxies: `http_proxy`, `https_proxy`, and `no_proxy` if they are set.
These are described in detail below:
- `https_proxy` a proxy URL for all https traffic. It may contain basic authentication credentials. For example:
  - http://proxy.com
  - http://127.0.0.1:8080
  - http://user:password@proxy.com
- `http_proxy` a proxy URL for all http traffic. It may contain basic authentication credentials. For example:
  - http://proxy.com
  - http://127.0.0.1:8080
  - http://user:password@proxy.com
- `no_proxy` a comma-separated list of hosts that should not use the proxy. An optional port may be specified. For example:
  - `google.com`
  - `yahoo.com:443`
  - `google.com,bing.com`

We won't use `http_proxy` for https traffic when `https_proxy` is not set, this behavior lines up with any libcurl based tools (curl, git) and wget.
Otherwise, action authors and workflow users need to adjust to differences between the runner proxy convention, and tools used by their actions and scripts.  

Example:  
  Customer sets `http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8888` and configures the runner against `https://github.com/owner/repo`, with the `https_proxy` -> `http_proxy` fallback, the runner will connect to the server without any problem. However, if a user runs `git push` to `https://github.com/owner/repo`, `git` won't use the proxy since it requires `https_proxy` to be set for any https traffic.

> `golang`, `node.js`, and other dev tools from the Linux community use `http_proxy` for both http and https traffic based on my research.

A majority of our users are using Linux where these variables are commonly required to be set by various programs. By reading these values, we simplify the process for self-hosted runners to set up a proxy and expose it in a way users are already familiar with.

A password provided for a proxy will be masked in the logs.

We will support the lowercase and uppercase variants, with lowercase taking priority if both are set.

Command echoing as a default behavior tends to clutter the user logs, so we want to swap to a system where users have to opt in to see this information.

Command outputs will still be echoed in the case there are any errors processing such commands. This is so the end user can have more context on why the command failed and help with troubleshooting.

## Decision 
We will disable command echoing by default to reduce log verbosity. Echoing will be enabled by default only when the `ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG` secret is set to `true`.

In the event of a command failure, the command output will always be echoed to the logs, regardless of the current echo setting. This ensures that users have sufficient context for troubleshooting failed steps. This change aims to make logs easier to read for successful runs while retaining full diagnostic information when errors occur.

## Context

- Provide a mechanism in the runner to include extra information in `Set up job` step's log.
  Ex: Include OS/Software info from Hosted image.
decision:
## Decision 
We will introduce a script-based hook mechanism in the runner to allow for the inclusion of arbitrary information in the `Set up job` log.

This will be implemented as follows:
1.  A new directory will be established on the runner host at `/home/runner/run.sh.d`.
2.  During the `Set up job` step, after the initial setup information is printed, the runner will scan this directory for any executable files.
3.  The runner will execute each script found, in lexicographical order.
4.  The standard output of each script will be redirected to the job log, prefixed with the script's filename for clarity and context. Standard error will also be redirected to the job log to aid in debugging faulty scripts.

This approach provides a generic and extensible hook for runner image maintainers to inject environment-specific information into the job setup log without requiring any changes to the runner binary itself. It is simple, transparent, and empowers users to add any information they deem relevant to their specific environment.

For example, to log the OS release information as requested, a file named `/home/runner/run.sh.d/10_os_release.sh` could be created with `+x` permissions and the following content:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
echo "OS Version Information:"
cat /etc/os-release
```

This would result in the contents of `/etc/os-release` being printed to the main job log during setup.

## Context

This ADR proposes adding `steps.<id>.outcome` and `steps.<id>.conclusion` to the steps context.

This allows downstream a step to run based on whether a previous step succeeded or failed.

Reminder, currently the steps contains `steps.<id>.outputs`.
decision:
## Decision
We will add `outcome` and `conclusion` fields to the `steps.<id>` context.

This will allow workflows to have conditional logic that depends on the success or failure of a specific, preceding step. Currently, a step's failure causes all subsequent steps to be skipped by default, but this change enables more granular control, such as running "clean-up" or notification steps only upon failure.

The new fields will be populated as follows:

*   `steps.<id>.conclusion`: The final status of the step. Will be one of `success`, `failure`, `cancelled`, or `skipped`.
*   `steps.<id>.outcome`: An alias for `steps.<id>.conclusion`. Both fields will contain the same value.

This functionality will be exposed via the standard `if` conditional on a step.

### Example Usage

```yaml
steps:
  - name: Build step
    id: build
    run: ./build.sh

  - name: Deploy on success
    if: steps.build.conclusion == 'success'
    run: ./deploy.sh

  - name: Notify on failure
    if: steps.build.conclusion == 'failure'
    run: ./notify-failure.sh
```

## Context
SS?? fundamentally relies on a third-party provider service to authenticate requests (e.g. OAuth2
via Google). The provider may experience transient faults for any number of reasons - perhaps the
provider is experiencing a transient outage, or our traffic has been temporarily rate limited. We
wanted to build SS?? to anticipate and handle the presence of faults during communication with
authentication providers, no matter the underlying cause.
decision:
## Decision 
We will implement a retry mechanism with exponential backoff and jitter for all requests to third-party authentication providers. This will make our service resilient to transient faults from the provider, such as temporary network issues, rate limiting, or brief outages.

The specific implementation will be as follows:
1.  When a request to a provider fails with a transient error (e.g., a 5xx server error, a timeout, or a 429 Too Many Requests), the service will not fail immediately.
2.  Instead, it will attempt to retry the request after a short delay.
3.  The delay will increase exponentially after each failed attempt. For example, the first retry might be after 100ms, the second after 200ms, the third after 400ms, and so on.
4.  Jitter (a small, random amount of time) will be added to each delay to prevent multiple instances of our service from retrying in a synchronized "thundering herd" pattern.
5.  We will configure a maximum number of retry attempts (e.g., 3 or 5). If all retries fail, the request will be considered failed, and an appropriate error response (e.g., 503 Service Unavailable) will be returned to the client.
predicted_decision:
## Decision
We implemented a generic `circuit.Breaker` type, which implements the "Circuit Breaker" design
pattern made popular by Michael T. Nygard's book, ["Release It!"](
https://pragprog.com/book/mnee/release-it). All requests to the provider service are issued through
a stateful `circuit.Breaker` instance, which tracks the frequency of request failures. When the
`Breaker` sees that enough requests are failing, it temporarily suspends all outgoing traffic to the
provider (i.e. "enters `Open` state). After some time, the `Breaker` transitions to a `HalfOpen`
state, in which a limited number of outbound requests are allowed. If failures persist, then the
`Breaker` will once again suspend outbound traffic, re-enter `Open` state, and typically will wait
for a longer interval of time before trying again. If instead the `Breaker` observes that requests
are consistently succeeding, then it will resume all outbound traffic (i.e. enter `Closed` state).

The SS?? [`docs`](/docs/) directory contains a [Circuit Breaker](
/docs/architecture/circuit-breaker.md) document with more details. The implementation can be found
in [`breaker.go`](/internal/auth/circuit/breaker.go)

## Context

Extensions are defined by an EDN file accessed from decentralized storage. An URI schema allows to identify those files.
decision:
## Decision 
We will use a dedicated URI scheme, `arachne-ext:`, to uniquely identify and locate the EDN files that define extensions.

This URI scheme provides a standard, location-agnostic way to refer to an extension's definition, regardless of the underlying decentralized storage mechanism. The resolution of these URIs will be handled by a pluggable resolver system, allowing Arachne to support various storage backends.

The structure of the URI will be `arachne-ext:<storage-backend>:<backend-specific-identifier>`.

Some examples include:

-   **IPFS:** An extension definition stored on the InterPlanetary File System would be identified by its Content Identifier (CID).
    -   `arachne-ext:ipfs:QmXoW8...`
-   **Git:** An extension defined in a specific file within a Git repository at a particular commit.
    -   `arachne-ext:git:github.com/arachne-framework/some-ext.git?path=config/extension.edn&rev=a1b2c3d4`
-   **Dat:** An extension stored in a Dat archive.
    -   `arachne-ext:dat:1a2b3c...//path/to/extension.edn`

This approach satisfies several goals:
-   **Modularity:** Modules can declare dependencies on extensions using these stable, unique identifiers without being coupled to a specific storage location or retrieval mechanism.
-   **Decentralization:** The scheme is explicitly designed to support a variety of decentralized (and centralized, like git/http) storage protocols.
-   **Verifiability:** Using content-addressable identifiers (like IPFS CIDs or Git commit hashes) ensures that the URI refers to a specific, immutable version of the extension definition, which is crucial for reproducibility and security.

## Decision

URI follows ethereum URI schema as specified in [EIP 831](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/blob/master/EIPS/eip-831.md)


```

path                    = "status:extension" ":" storage "@" id
storage                 = STRING (e.g. IPFS)
```

We want to launch our beta in Q2. This requires us to keep a tight scope and stay on the critical path.

Group chat is not as vital as 1-1 chat for the chat experience. It is also
likely not as useful for an MVP as public chat is, since this gives people a

decision:
## Decision 
Group chat functionality will be removed from the scope of the beta release.
This decision is made to ensure we can meet our Q2 beta launch goal by maintaining a tight scope and focusing on the critical path.
The rationale is as follows:
- **Priority:** 1-1 chat and public chat are more critical for a successful MVP.
- **Technical Debt:** There is a significant backlog of regressions related to group chat. Fixing these would divert essential resources from more critical features.
- **Complexity:** The encryption and security models for private group chats are inherently more complex and would introduce additional risk to the beta timeline.
- **Team Focus:** This provides a clear decision on a recurring topic, eliminating wasted effort in future discussions and allowing the team to focus on the core beta experience.

We will re-evaluate the inclusion of group chat after a successful beta launch.

## Context

Idea [142-Wallet-Compatibility](https://ideas.status.im/ideas/142-wallet-compatibility/README) changes the way we generate keys starting from the 12 mnemonic words.

This change allows users to create a wallet in other apps and import the same address in Status using the 12 mnemonic words.
decision:
## Decision 
We will adopt the standard BIP44 derivation path (`m/44'/60'/0'/0/x`) for all new accounts generated from a mnemonic phrase.

To ensure backward compatibility and prevent existing users from losing access to their funds, the application will also continue to support and scan for accounts on the old, non-standard derivation path.

The key generation and recovery logic will be updated as follows:
1.  **New Wallet Creation:** Any new wallet created within Status will use the BIP44 standard derivation path.
2.  **Wallet Recovery/Import:** When a user imports an account using a 12-word mnemonic, Status will scan for accounts on *both* the new standard BIP44 path and the legacy path to ensure all of the user's funds are discovered and accessible.

This change makes Status wallets compatible with most other Ethereum wallets (e.g., MetaMask, Ledger, Trezor), allowing for seamless import and export of accounts using the same mnemonic phrase.

* update the master key generation using the constant `"Bitcoin seed"` instead of `"status-im"`, following [BIP32](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0032.mediawiki#master-key-generation).

context:
## Context

On the path to releasing a usable beta we've faced a variety of performance
issues:

- https://github.com/status-im/ideas/issues/55
- https://ideas.status.im/ideas/071-low-traffic
- https://ideas.status.im/ideas/076-smooth-ui
- https://ideas.status.im/ideas/083-energy-efficient

Some of these performance issues are related to the use of LES, especially on
Mainnet. Examples of problems include: slow/hot sync, disk filling up, bandwidth
usage, etc. This can partly be remedied by the use of CHT to speed up sync
(https://github.com/status-im/status-go/wiki/Updating-CHT-BloomTrie).

In order to simplify the problem, we decided earlier this year to not spend too
much time looking into performance improvements related to LES, instead focusing
our efforts on improving the performance on Whisper and in client-side code.

This also means we don't have a full picture of to what extent LES is a
performance bottleneck for the Status app. It is possible proper use of CHT,
slowing sync down, vary load depending on if you are on WiFi or not, etc, can
solve these problems. However, the consensus right now is that ULC is the more
promising route to take.

However, since ULC isn't ready yet, this means we are relying on Infura. This
is a bad idea from a decentralization and security point of view. This can be
partly remedied by allowing the user to run an upstream node. It is still a bad
trust model, relying on third-party Ethereum nodes, and we want to get away
from this as soon as possible.

With ULC it is possible to connect to more than one node, which increases
decentralization and security.
decision:
## Decision 
We will deprecate LES and focus our efforts on ULC as the main way to connect to the Ethereum network.

While this means we are relying on Infura in the interim, which is not ideal from a decentralization and security point of view, we believe this is the right tradeoff to make. The main reasons for this are:

1.  **Performance**. There are several known performance issues with LES that negatively impact the user experience of the Status app.
2.  **Focus**. By focusing on one light client implementation, we can move faster and provide a better experience.
3.  **Decentralization and security**. ULC allows connecting to more than one node, which is a better security model than relying on a single node. This is not the case with our current LES mode.

In the short term, we will accept the reliance on a centralized service like Infura as a necessary step to deliver a performant, usable application. All resources previously dedicated to LES maintenance and improvement will be redirected to the development and integration of ULC to ensure we can move to a more decentralized and secure model as quickly as possible.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

1. Rely on upstream nodes for beta. For the closed beta scheduled to be releases
Q2 we will provide two ways of accessing the Ethereum network:

- Upstream RPC with Infura (default)
- Custom upstream node (https://github.com/status-im/status-mobile/issues/3994)

From a decentralization point of view we need the latter before we can release
the beta.

2. ULC MVP. Additionally, as soon as beta is released, assess and start to
   introduce ULC as an experimental non-default mode in the app.
   
By doing this we also support the network, since it is still a very new
protocol. ULC requires trusted peers to operate, and right now trust is
established by config (list of trusted peers).

Initially we could hardcode these nodes, with option to add your own. Later on
we can have some form of distributed directory with a rating system. This also
likely requires merging ULC upstream, so we aren't the only ones running trusted
nodes.

3. LES track (optional). If we still have resources and there's interest,
optionally run a parallel track to clean up LES usage (update CHT, cluster) and
understand exact performance impact and viablity of running LES on
resource-constrained devices.

These three decisions balances the following trade-offs:

- get a usable beta released as soon as possible
- provide users with options to get minimal amount of decentralization
- pave the way for trustless usage by default (ULC/LES node)

## Context

We have some data that we don't want to appear in the logs (user passwords are
a good example). Currently, they are passed around as strings, that could be
printed out by mistake in a log entry (see https://github.com/status-im/status-mobile/issues/4053)
decision:
## Decision 
We will introduce a new data type, `SensitiveString`, to represent data that should not be logged or otherwise displayed in plain text.

This type will have the following characteristics:
1.  It will act as a wrapper around a standard `String` value.
2.  Its `toString` method (or equivalent `print-method` in Clojure) will be overridden to return a placeholder value like `"[REDACTED]"`. This ensures that any logging framework or accidental `print` statement will not leak the sensitive information by default.
3.  A specific, explicitly named function (e.g., `unsecure-value`) will be provided to extract the raw, underlying string. The name of this function is intentionally chosen to make developers think twice before using it, reinforcing the sensitive nature of the data.
4.  All parts of the application that handle sensitive data (such as passwords, API keys, and personal identifiable information) will be refactored to use the `SensitiveString` type instead of a raw `String`.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

To minimize the risk of leaking passwords through logs, we should not pass
passwords as strings in our codebase. We introduced a new type `MaskedData` in
`status-im.utils.security`.
update (16-Dec-2022) `status-im.utils.security` is now moved over to `utils.security.core` 

We use `(security/mask-data <data to hide>` to wrap sensitive data into this
type and then use `(security/unmask <masked-data>)` to get the plaintext back.

It is important to keep that sensitive data masked as much as possible, until
you need the plaintext to pass to the extenral APIs.

Example:
```clojure
(println (security/mask-data "my-plaintext-password")) ;; Outputs "******"
(println (security/unmask (security/mask-data "my-plaintext-password"))) ;; Outputs "my-plaintext-password"
```

## Context

Originally, we supported 3rd party status extensions in form of javascript jailed execution environment (eq Jail) + small js library exposing chat commands API to js code.

While neat in theory, it has some serious downsides:

- Design of the API was quite poor, preferring mutable semantics over stateless API leveraging strength of the host application (cljs/re-frame).
  As a result of that, more dynamic/state requiring things (like the live tx detail in `/send` command messages) were very hard to do,
  so instead of "eating our own dogfood", we decided to side-step the API and implement such things as hard-coded logic in the app, while partly
  retaining the js code for "easier" things (like parameter declaration).
  Needles to say, such efforts produced code of very poor quality, riddling our app with hard-coded "magic" everywhere in the codebase, completely
  defeating the point of "dogfooding" while still requiring more effort and being much more error prone (no way to unit test jail logic) because 
  of the need to asynchronously communicate with jail for leftover logic in command messages (the parts not hardcoded in app).
  
- We were in a state where there was not even one command defined completely in jail, with all of them requiring custom hardcoded logic in app to
  actually work.
  Due to numerous changes and rush to get things working, half of the API was obsolete and was not working/working differently then described in
  the API documentation.
  
- We are quite tight stretched regarding performance and the Jail didn't particularly help with that - whenever some command message was defined in
  Jail, it required constant RN Bridge "ping-pong" whenever sending the message or receiving the message, eating more resources + breaking otherwise
  quite simple logic into harder to reason asynchronous call chains (execute method defined in Jail, wait for the result, execute next method in Jail...).
  
- Till now, there was no real interest in 3rd party bots anyway - the only "real" DAPPs submitted to status were "normal" DAPPs utilising just the `web3.js`
  API and built on top of regular web technologies, so they could be ran in any Ethereum client like Metamask or Mist, besides Status.
  
- There is a very promising new concept of extensions (project pluto), which will enable to extend status with much nicer and declarative extension
  definitions.
  Such extensions will not be able to only hook-in into the command messages logic, but also other application (host) hooks, like wallet assets/collectibles,
  chat contacts, etc.
decision:
## Decision 
We will deprecate and remove the legacy chat command extension system, including the Javascript "Jail" execution environment and its associated API.

All existing chat commands that partially relied on this system will be fully reimplemented as first-class components within the core ClojureScript application.

This change entails:
- Removing the jailed Javascript execution environment and all related bridge communication logic.
- Eliminating the chat commands API library that was exposed to the jail.
- Refactoring existing commands to be pure ClojureScript/re-frame code, removing the complex, asynchronous, and error-prone mix of hard-coded logic and jail communication.
- This will simplify the codebase, remove "magic" behavior, improve performance by eliminating RN Bridge overhead, and make command logic fully testable within our existing testing framework.

Future extensibility will be addressed by the new, more comprehensive extension system ("Project Pluto"), which offers a superior, declarative approach and broader integration capabilities beyond just chat commands. This decision allows us to stop investing in a failed approach and focus our efforts on the more promising future solution.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

In the light of points above, we decided to remove Jail and `Status.js` API from the application and re-work command messages in set of nicely
encapsulated app level protocols, so command related logic will be defined in one place, commands will be able to leverage strength of our platform
and development of any new functionality related to them will be much faster and more pleasant. 
We will address the 3rd party code issue separately by extensions.

## Context

The whitepaper describes Tribute to Talk (TtT) as an economics-based anti-spam filter for receiving messages and "cold" contact requests from user. Stakeholders would stake a minimum amount of SNT that another Status stakeholder must deposit in order to contact him directly.
The whitepaper also proposes that the deposit is only forfeited to the recipient if he replies.
decision:
## Decision 
We will implement the "Tribute to Talk" (TtT) feature as an economic anti-spam mechanism. A user (the "Recipient") can define a minimum amount of SNT that another user (the "Sender") must deposit to send them an initial contact request. The Sender's deposit will be held in escrow and is only forfeited to the Recipient if the Recipient replies to the initial message. If the Recipient does not reply, the deposit is returned in full to the Sender. This ensures that the tribute serves as an incentive for engagement, not just a barrier to contact.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

Considering:
- the absence of efficient ways to perform anonymous transactions (zk-snarks could be used in the future for that)
- the impossibility to prove that a recipient has made an actual reply and not some kind of automated reply (captcha solution was proposed, but wouldn't be practical until we can use a solution such as swarm feeds that allow users to make free updates to their captcha without on-chain transactions)
- the limited time to develop the feature

We opted for a solution that:
- doesn't establish a direct correlation between the tribute payment and an on-chain transaction, so it
- uses regular transactions for tributes payment, giving users plausible deniability about the nature of the payment
- doesn't store tribute information on-chain

## Context

During the development of a new Sylius API (based on API Platform) for Product Options, we had to decide how we should handle
Product Option's values collection, to make it efficient and easy to use.
decision:
## Decision 
We will handle the Product Option's values collection as a deeply nested object within the Product Option resource itself. Product Option Values will not be exposed as a separate, addressable API resource.

This means that to create, update, or delete a Product Option's values, the client will send a `POST` or `PUT` request to the parent Product Option's endpoint with the desired collection of values embedded in the request body.

The primary reasons for this decision are:

1.  **Ease of Use for the API Client:** Product options and their values are almost always managed as a single conceptual unit. Requiring the client to make separate API calls to create each value individually before associating them with the parent option would be cumbersome and complex. This approach allows a client to create a "Color" option and its "Red", "Green", and "Blue" values in a single, atomic `POST` request.

2.  **Efficiency:** This design reduces the number of network requests. Retrieving an option and all its values requires only one `GET` request. Similarly, updating the entire set of values can be done with a single `PUT` request.

The alternative considered was to expose Product Option Values as a separate API resource, linked as a subresource of the Product Option. This was rejected because it would lead to a "chattier" API, requiring multiple requests to perform common operations, complicating client-side logic, and being less efficient overall for this specific use case. While our chosen approach deviates from a strict RESTful model where every entity is an individually addressable resource, the practical benefits for the client in this context outweigh the adherence to that principle.

## Context and Problem Statement

A big chunk of resources available in Sylius have some part locale aware. Product descriptions, names of payment or shipping methods
should be translated to the customer to provide the best user experience. Right now most of the resources are returned with 
all available translations in the store and proper localization of content is left to the frontend developers. What is more,
this solution is not consistent, as some endpoints already embeds some part of translatables in them. We should provide clear,
easy to use and consistent way of handling customer locales.
decision:
## Decision 
We will implement a consistent, server-driven mechanism for API clients to request localized resource data, simplifying the experience for frontend developers. The API will be responsible for selecting the correct translation and returning a "flattened" resource representation.

The locale will be determined using the following order of precedence:

1.  **`localeCode` Query Parameter:** A client can explicitly request a locale by adding a query parameter to the GET request, e.g., `/api/v2/shop/products/MUG?localeCode=fr_FR`. This is the highest priority and will override any other mechanism. It is useful for explicit user actions (like a language switcher) and for ease of testing.
2.  **`Accept-Language` HTTP Header:** If no `localeCode` query parameter is provided, the server will inspect the standard `Accept-Language` header sent by the client. It will attempt to match the requested language(s) against the available translations for the resource.
3.  **Channel's Default Locale:** If neither of the above is provided, or if a translation for the requested locale does not exist, the API will fall back to using the default locale configured for the current channel.

The API response for localized resources will be changed to embed the selected translation directly into the top-level object, rather than returning all available translations.

**Example: Before this change**
A GET request to `/api/v2/shop/products/MUG` might return:
```json
{
    "code": "MUG",
    "translations": {
        "en_US": {
            "name": "Mug",
            "slug": "mug",
            "description": "A simple mug."
        },
        "fr_FR": {
            "name": "Tasse",
            "slug": "tasse",
            "description": "Une simple tasse."
        }
    }
}
```

**Example: After this change**
A GET request to `/api/v2/shop/products/MUG?localeCode=fr_FR` will return:
```json
{
    "code": "MUG",
    "name": "Tasse",
    "slug": "tasse",
    "description": "Une simple tasse."
}
```
This change will be applied consistently across all locale-aware resources in the API.
predicted_decision:
## Decision Outcome

The first approach should be used in admin section of API, while the third one should be used in shop section. This way, we
will receive best of both worlds with the minimal effort. It is worth mentioning that Sylius have two distinguish entry points
to API - admin and shop. They are concerned about different things and resolves different problems. Unified view of a product
in the shop will make it easy and straightforward to build product pages. At the same time all translation approach should be used in
admin to provide full control over "translation" resource - as we should treat them. Therefore, every resource translation
should be linked to the main resource through IRI. Each of these translation resource may be a subject of all CRUD operations
accessible throughout HTTP Verbs.

## Context

Decisions that affect the development of Terraform Controller that are not
captured via a proposal need to be captured in some way. We need a method that
is lightweight and easy to discover the decision that have been made. The record
of decisions will help future contributors to the project to understand why
something has been implemented or is done a certain way.
decision:
## Decision 
We will use Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to document architectural decisions for Terraform Controller.
ADRs are lightweight text documents that capture the context, decision, and consequences of a significant architectural choice. They will be stored as Markdown files within the project's source code repository.

### ADR Format
Each ADR will have a simple, consistent structure:
- **Title:** A short, descriptive name for the decision.
- **Status:** One of: `Proposed`, `Accepted`, `Rejected`, `Superseded`.
- **Context:** The problem, constraints, and forces at play that necessitate this decision.
- **Decision:** The chosen approach. This section should be clear and specific about what we are going to do.
- **Consequences:** The positive, negative, and neutral outcomes of making this decision. This includes trade-offs and any future work that may be required.

### Process
1. Any contributor can propose a decision by creating a new ADR file in a pull request with the status set to `Proposed`.
2. The team will discuss the proposal in the pull request. The ADR can be updated during this discussion.
3. Once consensus is reached, the ADR's status is changed to `Accepted` and the pull request is merged.
4. If a decision is later revisited, a new ADR will be created to supersede the old one. The old ADR's status will be updated to `Superseded by ADR-XXX`, preserving the historical record.

This approach provides a lightweight but effective way to document our decisions, making them easily discoverable and providing valuable context for all current and future contributors.

## Context

To detect pull request changes, we can use webhooks or polling using GitHub's
API.
decision:
## Decision 
We will use webhooks to detect pull request changes.

Polling would require us to constantly hit the GitHub API to check for changes. This is inefficient, introduces latency between a change and its detection, and would quickly exhaust our API rate limit.

Webhooks, by contrast, provide immediate, push-based notifications. This is a much more efficient and scalable approach. While it requires a publicly-accessible endpoint to receive the webhook, this is a standard and solvable architectural requirement. The benefits of real-time updates and conservation of API requests far outweigh this setup complexity.

We decided to start with polling for security reasons. Using webhooks would require users to
open an ingress to the cluster. Because of this requirement, we think security conscious folks may refuse to roll this out on production clusters especially in an
air-gapped environment. This does not mean that we will never consider using webhooks for this, but that initially, polling is what we have chosen to implement.

context:
## Context

Like [Flux](https://fluxcd.io/), the tf-controller API has a handful
of places where it accepts cross-namespace references.

 - `Terraform.spec.sourceRef` -- refers to the Flux source object with
   the Terraform program
 - `Terraform.spec.dependsOn[]` -- refers to other objects that must
   be ready before this object can be run
 - `.data.resources[]` -- in the config struct used by the branch
   planner

In general in Kubernetes, references to objects in other namespaces
are frowned upon, because

 - they break namespace isolation assurances; and,
 - they encourage the proliferation of permissions.

Both of these effects make a system less secure.

However: removing cross-namespace refs entirely would break some
installations in a way that would be difficult to fix, because Flux
deployments often rely on defining sources away from objects that use
them.
decision:
## Decision 
We will make the acceptance of cross-namespace references a configurable feature of the controller, which will be disabled by default.

A new controller flag, `--allow-cross-namespace-refs`, will be introduced.
- By default, this flag will be `false`. The controller's admission webhook will reject any `Terraform` object that specifies a `sourceRef`, `dependsOn`, or other entry pointing to an object in a different namespace. The rejection will be accompanied by a clear error message explaining the security implications and how to enable the feature if necessary.
- Cluster administrators who need to support this pattern for legacy or architectural reasons can enable the feature by setting the `--allow-cross-namespace-refs` flag to `true` in the controller's deployment arguments. This will restore the previous, more permissive behavior.

This approach strikes a balance between security and backward compatibility. It establishes a "secure by default" posture, enforcing namespace isolation for new installations and guiding users towards better security practices. At the same time, it provides a clear, explicit opt-in for existing users who rely on the feature, forcing an intentional decision by the administrator to relax these security constraints.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

Deny cross-namespace references by default, but allow them to be
enabled with a flag.

So that the default value means the right thing, the flag name must be

## Context

The TF-Controller currently faces challenges related to the deletion of Terraform resources.
These problems span across three categories:

1. Single object deletion,
2. Resources with dependencies deletion, and
3. Namespace deletion.

These problems must be fixed in the above order as (2) and (3) require single object deletion to be resolved first.

Deleting a single TF object can sometimes be obstructed because it's tied to other resources like Source objects, Secrets, and ConfigMaps. If we try to remove it without deleting these resources, the TF object gets stuck in an inconsistent state, making it harder for users to manage their infrastructure smoothly.
Therefore, the TF-Controller is being enhanced to address this problem more efficiently, using the contents of generated Workspace BLOBs. Each BLOB contains all necessary information from the associated Source, Secrets, and ConfigMaps to ensure that TF-Controller finalization procedures can delete objects correctly.

Currently, the TF-Controller downloads a Source BLOB and pushes it to a tf-runner. The tf-runner processes this BLOB to create a Workspace file system. It generates a backend configuration file, variable files, and other necessary files for the Workspace file system, using data from associated Secrets and ConfigMaps. This newly created Workspace file system is then compressed, sent back to the TF-Controller, and stored as a Workspace BLOB in the controller's storage.
A caching mechanism for these BLOBs is essential to fixing the single TF object deletion process.
decision:
## Decision 
We will implement a caching mechanism for Workspace BLOBs within the TF-Controller. This cache will store the fully-hydrated Terraform workspace, including all necessary configurations from associated Source, Secrets, and ConfigMaps.

The primary goal is to ensure that the TF-Controller's finalizer has access to a complete and self-contained workspace, enabling it to successfully execute a `terraform destroy` operation even if the dependent Kubernetes resources (Sources, Secrets, ConfigMaps) are no longer available. This approach decouples the deletion lifecycle of a Terraform resource from its dependencies, directly addressing the issue of objects getting stuck in an inconsistent state during finalization.

The workflow will be as follows:

1.  **BLOB Generation and Caching**: During the normal reconciliation loop of a Terraform object, after the `tf-runner` has successfully created a compressed Workspace file system (the "Workspace BLOB"), it is sent back to the TF-Controller. The TF-Controller will then persist this BLOB in its own storage, effectively caching it for the lifetime of the object.
2.  **Finalization on Deletion**: When a user requests deletion of a Terraform custom resource, the finalizer on the object will prevent its immediate removal.
3.  **Using the Cache**: The TF-Controller's finalization logic will retrieve the cached Workspace BLOB from its storage. It will *not* attempt to re-fetch the original Source, Secrets, or ConfigMaps.
4.  **Executing Destroy**: The self-contained Workspace BLOB is passed to a `tf-runner` instance with instructions to perform a `terraform destroy`.
5.  **Completion**: Upon successful destruction of the underlying infrastructure, the TF-Controller removes its finalizer from the Terraform object, allowing the Kubernetes garbage collector to complete the deletion.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

1. **BLOB Creation and Storage**
   * A gRPC function named `CreateWorkspaceBlob` will be invoked by the TF-Controller 
     to tell tf-runner to compress the Workspace file system into a tar.gz BLOB, which is then retrieved back to the controller.
   * The caching mechanism will be executed right before the Terraform Initialization step, ensuring that the latest and most relevant data is used.
   * Each Workspace Blob will be cached on the TF-Controller's local disk, using the UUID of the Terraform object as the filename,`${uuid}.tar.gz`.
   * To reduce the risk of unauthorized access to the cache entries, and cache collisions, the cache file will be deleted after the finalization process is complete.
2. **Persistence** 
   * [The persistence mechanism used by the Source Controller](https://fluxcd.io/flux/installation/configuration/vertical-scaling/#persistent-storage-for-flux-internal-artifacts) will be adopted for the TF-Controller's persistence volume.
3. **BLOB Encryption**
   * The encryption and decryption of the BLOBs will be tasked to the runner, with the controller solely responsible for storing encrypted BLOBs.
   * Each namespace will require a service account, preferably named "tf-runner".
   * The token of this service account, which is natively supported by Kubernetes, will serve as the most appropriate encryption key because it's stored in a Secret, access to which can be controlled by RBAC. Storing it in a Secret also allows the key to be rotated.
4. **Security Measures (Based on STRIDE Analysis)**
   * **Spoofing:** Implement Kubernetes RBAC for access restrictions and use mutual authentication for gRPC communications.
   * **Tampering:** Use checksums for integrity verification and 0600 permissions to write-protect local disk storage.
   * **Repudiation:** Ensure strong logging and auditing mechanisms for tracking activities.
   * **Information Disclosure:** Utilize robust encryption algorithms, rotate encryption keys periodically, and secure service account tokens.
   * **Denial of Service:** Monitor storage space and automate cleanup processes.
   * **Elevation of Privilege:** Minimize permissions associated with service account tokens.
5. **First MVP & Future Planning**
   * For the initial MVP, the default pod local volume will be used.
   * Since a controller restart will erase the BLOB cache, consideration for using persistent volumes should be made for subsequent versions.

## Context

In previous releases of Zarf, the creation of the initialization package at the core of many of our E2E tests required repository secrets to login to registry1. Since this is an open-source project, anyone could submit a change to one of our GitHub workflows that could steal our secrets. In order to protect our secrets from any bad-actors we used [peter-evans/slash-command-dispatch@v2](https://github.com/peter-evans/slash-command-dispatch) so that only a maintainer would have the ability to run the E2E tests when a PR is submitted for review.

In the current version of Zarf (v0.15) images from registry1 are no longer needed to create the zarf-init-{{arch}}.tar.zst. This means, given our current span of E2E tests, we no longer need to use repository secrets when running tests. This gives us the ability to reassess the way we do our E2E testing.

When considering how to handle the tests, some of the important additions we were considering were:
  1. Ability to test against different kubernetes distributions
  2. Ability to test against different linux distributions
  3. Ability to run (at least some of) the E2E tests locally without relying on an ec2 instance - for quicker feedback loops when developing new features
decision:
## Decision 
We will replace the maintainer-invoked `slash-command-dispatch` workflow with a fully automated E2E test suite that runs on every pull request.
This change is motivated by the removal of the `registry1` secret dependency for creating the init-package in Zarf v0.15, which was the original reason for protecting the E2E test runs.
To meet our new testing goals, the workflow will be implemented as follows:
1.  A GitHub Actions matrix strategy will be used to run the E2E tests across a variety of Kubernetes and Linux distributions on each PR. This will provide broader, more immediate feedback on the compatibility of any proposed changes.
2.  The E2E test suite will be designed to be fully runnable on a local developer machine. This will provide a much faster feedback loop during development, as contributors can validate their changes without needing to push a PR and wait for a cloud runner.
This new approach removes the manual bottleneck of waiting for a maintainer, increases our test coverage, and significantly improves the developer experience by providing faster, more accessible feedback.

## Decision

The previous E2E test code was not extensible enough to be reused to test Zarf against different kubernetes distributions. The test suite was refactored so that we could write a setup and teardown function for each kubernetes distribution we wanted to verify against and the test suite was then responsible for cycling through the different distributions. This gives us the ability to test multiple kubernetes distributions against the same exact test cases.

The individual test cases were also rewritten to not rely on terratest running a bash command over ssh. Instead, the test uses the locally built Zarf binary and example packages to validate expected behavior. This approach works both on local dev machines (linux/mac) and on the Ubuntu GitHub Runner that gets triggered when a pull request is created. This also has the positive side effect of not needing to wait several minutes for an ec2 instance to spin up for testing.

Since we no longer need repository secrets to run the E2E tests, we removed the requirement for a maintainer to use a `/test all` chatops command to dispatch the tests. Instead, there is a new test workflow defined for each kubernetes distribution we are verifying against and the tests get run automatically whenever a PR is created or updated.

When looking back at the list of 'important additions' we were considering above. All three are addressed with this approach. Testing against different kubernetes distributions is as simple as defining how to create and destroy the cluster. All of the test cases are runnable locally and then because of that testing on a linux distribution is possible by just switching over to another machine and running the same `make test-e2e` there. This also gives us the ability to test against cloud distributions like EKS! All you need is a valid kubeconfig and running `go test ./...` in the `./src/test/e2e` directory will run all of the test cases against the EKS cluster.
